prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at the magic wavelength brought optical frequency standards to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for the optical lattice clock to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. Nothing in the other seven statements weakened the physics, and the chair's questions let me state the case more sharply. The discovery is a concrete one that I can check against how real devices behave: at the magic wavelength the light shift of the two clock states cancels, so thousands of neutral atoms are held tightly, free of Doppler and recoil shifts, and interrogated in parallel. That parallelism is what turned an idea into a clock whose statistical resolution lets one find and remove systematic shifts at the 10^-18 level. This has been reproduced and compared across independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE, NPL), including over fibre links, which is the robustness test I apply to every result in my own field. It opens a new regime, not just a better number: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on drifts of constants, and dark-matter searches. The credit is two names with two distinct roles, concept and first demonstration (Katori) and record realisation and many-body clock work (Ye), and all members who ranked it name the same pair. On the chair's question about the redefinition of the second, I treat it as a consequence of the discovery rather than a precondition: the physics was established when independent clocks agreed at 10^-18, and the Academy rewards the discovery, not the metrological decision of the CIPM.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection remains overlap with the 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch, frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (Wineland and Haroche, control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks). I have asked myself whether the lattice clock is merely a refinement of those. I conclude it is not, for a physical reason: the comb supplied the counting mechanism and ion clocks demonstrated optical clocks with one particle, whereas the lattice clock solved the problem of combining many atoms with an unperturbed transition, which is a different principle and the one that delivered the stability. The wording of the citation should therefore name the magic-wavelength lattice and the 10^-18 level, not optical clocks in general. The second objection is early-developer credit (Lemonde, Pal'chikov, Takamoto, Ludlow). I cannot adjudicate atomic-physics priority and defer to Lindroth, Kroll and Olsson, but in my reading those contributions are demonstrations or extensions of Katori's proposal, and the Statutes limit us to three names anyway. The pending redefinition of the second is a timing worry I do not regard as decisive.

responses.point: Lindroth holds B012 first, sees credit separation from the 2005 and 2012 prizes as manageable, asks whether a citation naming the magic-wavelength lattice separates the work from them, and asks whether Lemonde and other pioneers displace Katori or Ye.
responses.response: Your magic-wavelength wording is the right one, and I would adopt it. As a theorist working with experimental groups, I find the distinction convincing in physical terms: the 2012 ion clocks have one particle, so they never face the problem of a many-atom lattice with a cancelled light shift. That problem and its solution are Katori's. On early developers, I defer to you on priority, but I note that your own round-1 statement describes Katori's idea and Ye's realisation as two distinct roles, and I do not see you naming anyone who proposed the magic-wavelength condition independently and then built the clock. If you do see such a case, please say so plainly now, because it is the one point that could change the pair.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first and B012 second as an alternative, valuing a clean theory-then-experiment sequence and many independent groups confirming it.
responses.response: I agree that Bistritzer and MacDonald followed by the 2018 observation is a compelling sequence, and in round 1 I accepted that B042 would be a respectable outcome. After reading Mehlig's reply to me I will concede one thing: the mechanism of the superconductivity need not be settled for the discovery of correlated states at the magic angle to count, as with the cuprates. My remaining difference with you is about the credit and the maturity, not the physics. Yuan Cao, who did the 2018 experiments, is outside the three names, and Mehlig, Eriksson and you each concede that B012 is the more settled choice. I am therefore listing B042 as my first alternative, which I did not do in round 1. If you and Eriksson want to say what would make it ready, such as a settled account of the insulating states, I would listen.

responses.point: Mehlig answers my round-1 reservation by arguing the discovery does not require the superconducting mechanism and that twist-angle disorder is a quantitative nuisance, while conceding that B042 is weakest on maturity relative to older platforms; he also notes the three-person limit makes a two-achievement prize impractical.
responses.response: That is a fair answer and it moves me part of the way: I accept that the pairing mechanism is a follow-up question and not a precondition, and I withdraw the weight I put on it in my opening ranking. Your own concession about maturity is the point I keep. For a theorist, the continuum model is attractive precisely because it is simple and checkable, but the experiment that gave it force is reproduced with real sample dependence, whereas for clocks cross-laboratory agreement at 10^-18 is a quantitative test that is already passed. I agree with you that a two-part prize is impractical under the three-person limit, so I am not proposing one.

responses.point: Kroll asks whether the first lattice-clock demonstrations and the many-body clock work should be described separately in the citation, and holds B020 as his first alternative while sharing my timing worry about B005.
responses.response: On the citation I would keep a single achievement with one sentence and not split it: Katori's concept and first demonstration and Ye's record accuracy and many-body clock work are two roles in one invention, and splitting them would invite a debate over Takamoto and Ludlow that we cannot resolve and the Statutes do not require. I also thank you for your deference on B005; given my WACQT role I will not argue for it this year. On B020, I agree it is credible, but I have kept it as a second alternative only, because the 2012 overlap and the Wineland and Monroe credit problem you mention are real.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asks whether Ye's contribution is central enough to justify his place, and asked me which quantum-information candidate has the fewest credit overlaps.
responses.response: Ye's place is justified in my view. The strontium lattice clock at JILA is what first showed the 10^-18 regime in a way other laboratories reproduced, and his group's work on many-body effects in the lattice and on linking clocks through frequency combs is part of why the number is believed. Without Ye the citation would reward a proposal and early demonstration but not the realisation. On your question to me: among the quantum-information candidates, I would say none is cleaner than B012. Trapped ions (B020) overlap with 2012, Rydberg arrays (B019) look like a platform still in development, and circuit QED (B005) has the timing problem and the Girvin and transmon-inventor credit problem, which is why I no longer advocate for it.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the magic-wavelength lattice is distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. I think it is, but this is a judgement of the committee and not mine alone.
Whether any early lattice-clock worker (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow) has a priority claim that should displace or add to Katori or Ye; I defer to Lindroth, Kroll and Olsson.
Whether to wait for the redefinition of the second. I would not wait, but I recognise that others weigh timing differently.
Whether B042 would be seen as ready by those who prefer it; I have no expertise to judge the insulating states and defer to Eriksson, Mehlig and Danielsson.
statement.conflict_note: I am director of WACQT (Chalmers), a national programme in superconducting quantum computing, and I work professionally in circuit QED. That is a field-proximity and possible institutional interest in B005 (Blais, Wallraff, Schoelkopf), and to a lesser extent in B020 and B019 as quantum-computing platforms. I no longer prefer B005, but I would recuse myself or discount my own view if it came back into the discussion, and I do not rely on it for any argument above. I have no personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer, so no conflict is apparent for B012 or B042. Eva Olsson's Chalmers colleague relationship with me is noted and does not bear on B012.
